speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: asked	the Minister for National Development (a) what are the impediments to releasing the Cross Island MRT Line (CIL) Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) 	Page: 17 Phase 1 report online; (b) what are the main environmental impact the EIA has identified about the site investigations preceding construction of the CIL through the Central Catchment Nature Reserve Area and how the Ministry intends to mitigate them; and (c) how is the "moderate" impact from the CIL (assuming successful mitigation measures) determined and what is the reasoning for why this is acceptable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When LTA first announced the possible alignment of the CRL in 2013, nature groups understandably, raised concerns about the potential serious environmental impact that this may have on the Central Catchment Nature Reserve (CCNR).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Because of these concerns, LTA formed a working group to define the scope of the EIA study of the CRL.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This working group included representatives of nature groups.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NParks also participated in the working group to provide views, inputs and the expertise.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Separately, a group made up of residents staying around the CCNR expressed concern about how the possible alignments may affect their homes and LTA has been engaging them as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Over the course of more than two years, LTA consulted the nature groups extensively in preparing for Phase 1 of the EIA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, in studying the impact of the proposed site investigation works on the water quality, ecology and biodiversity within the Nature Reserve, LTA's EIA consultant took into consideration a very useful baseline study on various aspects of the CCNR which was put together by our nature groups.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As indicated in the Phase 1 EIA report, the impact assessment framework adopted by LTA's EIA consultant has two criteria.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: One, the sensitivity of the receptor, which is the CCNR in this case, and two, the magnitude of the environmental impact on the ground.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, if Members look at the handout: look at the x-axis – it talks about the sensitivity of the receptor; the y-axis – refers to the magnitude of the environmental impact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is a framework which the EIA consultant uses to band an impact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: LTA's EIA consultant has rated the sensitivity of the CCNR as "high", as it comprises primary rainforest with ecologically sensitive habitats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While this is so, the consultant has assessed the magnitude of impact due to the site investigation to be mainly "small".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is because of the adoption of stringent mitigating measures that had been proposed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These mitigation measures were arrived at in close consultation with several representatives of the nature groups and NParks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Both groups saw the report before it was published.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Page: 18 Let me briefly describe what the site investigation entails and what mitigation measures have been proposed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The site investigation adopts two methods to determine the geological properties of the site.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The first method is borehole drilling, by which, boreholes, about 10 centimetres in diameter, are drilled to extract vertical columns of soil and rock samples.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And the drilling machine will be modified to reduce the noise level and prevent spillage of slurry and fuel.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To make up for the drastic reduction in the number of boreholes and because boreholes will be restricted only to the trails, a second method of site investigation will be carried out.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To carry this out, surveyors will venture off-trail into the forest to collect data using hand-held equipment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will be of significantly lower impact than actual borehole drilling in the forest.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, they will manpack the equipment into the forest and they will place it on the ground to detect the signals and to determine the geology of the ground at the location.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: One of the concerns is that the surveyors may inadvertently trample on plants on the forest floor as they move through dense vegetation off-trail.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The geophysical survey is therefore limited to a 100-metre wide corridor and will not be carried out in sensitive locations such as streams, swamps and dense vegetation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NParks officers will supervise the surveyors full-time to ensure that they adhere to the strict rules for movements in off-trail forested areas and to reduce damage from trampling on plants and vegetation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: All site investigation activities will be restricted to daylight hours, so as not to affect nocturnal animals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These stringent measures have been incorporated into the Phase 1 EIA report, which will reduce the impact of the site investigation to a level that is as low as reasonably practicable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A great amount of effort has been put in by all parties – representatives of nature groups, NParks and LTA – to arrive at this set of mitigation measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The on-going public consultation for the EIA report – and this report has been put online – allows the public an opportunity to provide further suggestions to LTA on what more can be done to further reduce the impact of the site investigation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The information I am referring to includes all the costs, the environmental impact, the commuting time impact and so on and so forth, when the information is ready, when the Phase 2 of the EIA is done and so on and so forth.
